items.stem: Tariq writes the equation of a line as r = (1, 0, −5) + λ(1, 1, −3) and a friend writes r = (4, 3, −14) + μ(−1, −1, 3). Explain why both equations describe the same line.
items.answer: Same direction (parallel) and a common point.
items.markingKey: Direction vectors are parallel: (−1, −1, 3) = −1(1, 1, −3) (R1); the point (4, 3, −14) lies on the first line with λ = 3 (M1 A1); so the lines coincide (R1).

items.stem: Define the term "right-hand rule".
items.answer: The convention fixing the direction of v × w: v, w and v × w form a right-handed set

items.stem: Explain how to decide whether the point Q(3, 0, 4) lies in the plane x + 4y − z = 3, and give the conclusion.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the direction of the line of intersection of two planes is n₁ × n₂.
items.answer: The line lies in both planes so it is perpendicular to both normals; n₁ × n₂ is perpendicular to both.

items.stem: Arjun writes the equation of a line as r = (−1, 0, 4) + λ(2, 2, 3) and a friend writes r = (3, 4, 10) + μ(−2, −2, −3). Explain why both equations describe the same line.
items.answer: Same direction (parallel) and a common point.
items.markingKey: Direction vectors are parallel: (−2, −2, −3) = −1(2, 2, 3) (R1); the point (3, 4, 10) lies on the first line with λ = 2 (M1 A1); so the lines coincide (R1).

items.stem: Noah says that L₁: r = (1, −6, 1) + λ(−1, −2, 1) and L₂: r = (6, −4, −5) + μ(−3, 3, 0) must meet because their direction vectors are not parallel. Explain why this reasoning is wrong for lines in 3D, and show that these lines are in fact skew.
items.markingKey: In 3D non-parallel lines need not meet (R1); equate components and solve two equations for λ and μ (M1); the third equation is not satisfied (A1); so the lines are skew (R1).

items.stem: Without computing it fully, explain why (1, −1, −3) × (−2, 2, 6) = 0.

items.answer: The angle between lines is taken as the acute angle: use |d₁·d₂| in the numerator.

items.stem:

items.answer: (0, −2, −2); the determinant of the coefficient matrix is −15 ≠ 0 (normals not coplanar), so the solution is unique

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "direction vector"?
options: Any non-zero vector parallel to a line
V × w, the vector perpendicular to both v and w with magnitude |v||w| sin θ and direction given by the right-hand rule
|v × w|, where v and w are adjacent sides
Non-parallel lines that share exactly one point
items.answer: Any non-zero vector parallel to a line

items.answer: The two vectors AB and AC lie in the plane; their vector product is perpendicular to both, so it is a normal to the plane.

items.stem: Explain why the vector equation of a line is not unique.
items.answer: Any point on the line can be used as a, and any non-zero multiple of the direction vector can be used as b, giving different-looking equations of the same line.

items.answer: First compare direction vectors: multiples → parallel (check a common point for coincidence). Otherwise equate components, solve two equations for λ and μ, and test the third: consistent → intersecting, inconsistent → skew.
